title: How Sport Built My Leadership Before I Knew I Was Leading
author: Paul Robinson
summary: Paul Robinson, a PE teacher and coach, traces how playing and coaching football shaped his approach to leadership. He begins with a trial where a coach made him captain within minutes, an early act of trust that set him on a path toward coaching and teaching. He is candid about his early coaching mistakes, including shouting, talking too much, wanting to be liked and treating every loss as a personal verdict. Becoming a PE teacher shifted his focus from performance to people, and his philosophy moved from control to trust, from outcomes to process and from blame to ownership. He now takes responsibility when a player errs while following instructions, so that players feel safe to take risks. His closing claim is that real leadership is built over time, often long before one realises one is leading.
points: A single act of trust from a coach, naming a hesitant teenager captain, can change the direction of a person’s whole leadership path.
Sport exposes weakness, and the author’s early habits of shouting, seeking validation and taking results personally are presented as a baseline from which to grow.
His philosophy moved from control to trust, from outcomes to process and from blame to ownership, with the leader accepting responsibility for mistakes made while following instructions.
Psychological safety to take risks, ask questions and make decisions is described as the condition in which real development happens.
Progress, measured by comparing a final performance with a first one, is offered as a healthier standard than winning for relieving pressure on coaches.
quotes: Sport, whether playing or coaching, has a way of exposing your weaknesses. As a young and naïve coach, I made plenty of mistakes — the kind I now look back on and cringe.
But more importantly, that coach invested time in me. He saw something I didn’t yet see in myself — and in many ways, set me on the path towards coaching, mentoring and teaching.
Every loss felt personal. Every result felt like a judgement. My dad would often say, “Why are you taking this so much to heart?
I moved away from control and towards trust. From outcomes to process. From blame to ownership.
If a player made a mistake trying to do what I had asked, I took responsibility. Not them. I wanted players to feel safe to take risks.
If there’s improvement, then progress has been made. And if progress has been made, then you’re doing your job.
Because leadership — real leadership — isn’t something you switch on. It’s something that’s built, often long before you realise you’re leading at all.
